lessons.t: Noticing what you feel right now
lessons.intro: You will learn to pause and name the emotion you are having at this moment. Naming a feeling is the first skill of emotional intelligence, because you cannot manage what you have not noticed.

cards.b: Emotions often show up as body signals first, such as a tight chest or a warm face. Notice the signal before you try to explain it.
Take three slow breaths and ask yourself what is happening inside you. This short pause gives your thinking time to catch up with your body.
Ask whether you feel pleasant or unpleasant, and whether your energy is high or low. These two questions sort most moods into a clear region.

fig.title: Noticing a feeling
fig.note: Three breaths, then a single word for the feeling.

ex.q: You feel your jaw clench and your chest tighten before a meeting. Which step comes first in noticing this feeling?
ex.why: The first step is to pause and notice the physical signal. Naming the feeling comes after you have registered what your body is telling you.

lessons.tip: Name the feeling in one word, such as worried, bored or proud.

quiz.q: Which two questions help sort most moods?
o: Is it sunny and is it late
Is it pleasant and is energy high or low
Who is near and what time is it
Am I hungry and am I tired
quiz.why: Pleasant versus unpleasant and high versus low energy map most moods on a simple grid.

quiz.q: Why do emotions often appear first in the body?
o: The body thinks faster than the mind
Feelings are triggered by physical signals first
Words are always slower than muscles
quiz.why: Bodily signals such as a tight chest often register before you can put the feeling into words.

lessons.intro: You will learn to replace vague words like bad or fine with more exact feeling words. Precise labels make it easier to understand what you need and to explain it to others.

cards.b: Saying I feel bad covers everything from disappointed to humiliated. Each of these needs a different response, so a precise word points you to the right one.
Group feelings into families such as anger, sadness, fear and joy, then list the milder and stronger versions. Keep a short list on your phone to use when you need it.

cards.h: Rate intensity from one to ten
cards.b: Give the feeling a number from one to ten to show how strong it is. A three of annoyance and an eight of rage call for very different actions.

fig.title: Same day, different feelings
fig.note: Each label names a stronger version of the same signal.

ex.q: Which description is most precise?
o: I feel disappointed that the plan changed
ex.why: Naming the specific feeling and its cause tells you what happened and what might help. Bad, off or something give no direction at all.

lessons.tip: Swap one vague word for a precise one each time you talk about your day.

quiz.q: Which word is milder than furious?
quiz.why: Irritated is a milder form of anger, while furious sits at the top of that range.

quiz.q: Why rate a feeling from one to ten?
o: To judge how strong the feeling is
quiz.why: A number shows how strong the feeling is, which helps you choose a proportionate response.

lessons.intro: You will learn to recognise the situations, words and people that reliably set off your feelings. Knowing your triggers gives you a chance to respond on purpose instead of by habit.

cards.b: Triggers often involve feeling ignored, criticised, rushed or treated unfairly. Look back at the last three strong reactions and see whether one of these themes appears.
Note the situation, the feeling and its strength each time you react strongly. Within a week, repeated patterns usually become obvious.
Having a trigger does not mean something is wrong with you. It means you have a sensitivity worth understanding and planning for.

fig.title: Reacting or responding
fig.note: A trigger sets off the first. Awareness helps you choose the second.

ex.q: Over a week you notice that you snap whenever someone interrupts you. What is the most useful next step?
o: Wait until the feeling passes forever
Name the trigger and plan a response for interruptions
ex.why: Naming the trigger lets you prepare a calmer response for that exact situation. Avoiding conversations or blaming others does not build any skill.

lessons.tip: Your triggers are information, not verdicts about your character.

quiz.q: How long is a useful tracking period for triggers?
quiz.why: A week of notes is usually enough to show repeated patterns without becoming a burden.

quiz.q: Which is a common trigger theme?
quiz.why: Feeling ignored, criticised, rushed or treated unfairly are frequent themes behind strong reactions.

lessons.intro: You will learn how common physical signals like a racing heart, shallow breath or clenched hands point to specific emotions. Reading these signals early gives you a head start on understanding your mood.

cards.b: Anger and fear often speed up the heart and shorten the breath. Sadness is more likely to slow your energy and make breathing feel heavy.
Clenched jaws, raised shoulders and tight stomachs are frequent signs of stress. Relaxing those muscles on purpose can ease the feeling a little.
Scan from head to toe once a day and note any tension. Recording what you find helps you connect body states with the feelings that follow.

fig.title: Body signal loop
fig.note: Each pass through the loop shortens the gap between signal and choice.

ex.q: Your shoulders are raised, your jaw is tight and your breathing is quick. Which emotion do these signs most often suggest?
ex.why: Raised shoulders, a tight jaw and quick breath are common signs of stress. Calm would show loose muscles and slow, steady breathing.

lessons.tip: Your body often knows a feeling a few seconds before your mind does.

quiz.q: What often happens to breathing during fear?
quiz.why: Fear and anger commonly speed up breathing as the body prepares to act.

quiz.q: What is a useful body check?
o: Scan from head to toe once a day
quiz.why: A short daily scan helps you notice tension and connect it with the feelings behind it.

lessons.intro: You will learn to separate what you feel from what you think about a situation. This distinction stops a passing thought from being mistaken for a fact about your life.

cards.b: A feeling is a state such as anxious or hurt, while a thought is a story such as nobody likes me. Mixing them up makes feelings seem like proof.
Words like should, must and always often hide a thought that is driving a feeling. Notice those words and ask whether the rule is actually true.
Ask what facts support the thought and what facts argue against it. A thought with little evidence can be held more loosely.

fig.title: The chain from event to action
fig.note: Feelings follow the story you tell, not the event alone.

ex.q: Your friend did not reply to a message, and you think they are angry with you. Which part is the feeling?
ex.why: Worried names a feeling you have, while the other options are either a story about someone else or a plain fact. Separating these parts shows which thing you can actually work with.

lessons.tip: A feeling describes you right now, while a thought is a story you can question.

quiz.q: Which sentence is a thought rather than a feeling?
quiz.why: Nobody cares about me is a story about other people, while the others name states you experience.

quiz.q: What helps test a thought?
o: Listing evidence for and against it
quiz.why: Weighing evidence for and against a thought shows how well supported it really is.

lessons.intro: You will learn to keep a simple log of your emotions across the day. Patterns that are invisible in one moment become clear when you look at several days together.

cards.b: Each entry needs three things: the event, the feeling and its strength. Keep entries short so you will actually keep doing it.
Choose two or three moments each day, such as midday and bedtime, to check in. Regular timing makes your record more honest than occasional notes.
Read the week's entries and circle any feeling that appears more than twice. Repeated feelings point to where to focus your attention next.

fig.title: Weekly mood log
fig.note: Repeated tension after email is worth a closer look.

ex.q: Over a week you log tension on four of seven days, mostly after emails. What is the best conclusion?
o: Tension links to emails and is worth a plan
You have no patterns at all
Tension is random and can be ignored
ex.why: Four of seven days with tension after emails shows a repeated link worth addressing. Calling emails always harmful goes further than the data support.

lessons.tip: A short log kept daily beats a long log kept once.

quiz.q: How many check-ins per day does the lesson suggest?
quiz.why: Two or three fixed check-ins keep the log regular without becoming a chore.

quiz.q: What should each log entry include?
o: Your full diary of the day
A list of other people's faults
quiz.why: Event, feeling and strength are enough to reveal useful patterns over time.

lessons.intro: You will learn how strong feelings often point to something you care about, such as fairness, respect or safety. Understanding the value behind a feeling makes it easier to act in line with what matters to you.

cards.b: Anger often means a value like fairness has been crossed, and sadness often points to something you cherish being lost. Ask what the feeling is protecting.
When a feeling is strong, ask what you wanted from the situation. The answer usually names a value such as honesty, kindness, control or growth.
Write down five values that matter most to you, in order. When a feeling flares, check whether it is serving one of these or working against it.

fig.title: Following a strong feeling
fig.note: Each step turns a reaction into a considered choice.

ex.q: You feel furious when a colleague takes credit for your work. Which value is most likely behind the anger?
ex.why: Anger at credit being taken usually signals that fairness and recognition matter to you. The other options do not connect to the situation described.

lessons.tip: Behind almost every strong feeling is a value you care about.

quiz.q: What does sadness often point to?
quiz.why: Sadness often reflects the loss or threat of something you care about.

quiz.q: What is a good first question when a feeling is strong?
o: What did I want from this?
quiz.why: Asking what you wanted reveals the value underneath the feeling.

lessons.intro: You will learn what your emotional baseline is and how to tell it apart from temporary mood swings. Knowing your usual state helps you notice when something has shifted.

cards.b: Everyone has a typical level of calm, energy and worry that they return to most days. Your baseline is shaped by sleep, work, health and habits.
A shift from your usual state is worth attention even when it is not extreme. Two or three days of unusual flatness or edginess are a useful early signal.
Think back over a normal week and describe your mood in a few words. Comparing today with that description shows whether you are drifting.

fig.title: Feelings logged in one week
fig.note: Counts of logged feelings, showing a usual baseline.

ex.q: Your usual mood is steady, but for four days you feel unusually flat and snappy. What does this suggest?
o: You have a new baseline forever
A shift from your normal state worth noticing
ex.why: A sustained change from your usual pattern is a signal worth paying attention to, even if it is not severe. Your steady baseline is the reference that makes the change visible.

lessons.tip: Know your normal so you can spot when you have drifted from it.

quiz.q: What shapes a person's emotional baseline?
quiz.why: Sleep, work, health and daily habits all influence your typical emotional state.

quiz.q: How many unusual days might be an early signal?
quiz.why: Two or three days of unusual mood can be a useful early signal worth noticing.

lessons.intro: You will learn to distinguish guilt, which is about something you did, from shame, which is about who you feel you are. The difference shapes whether you repair a situation or retreat from it.

cards.b: Guilt says I did something that hurt someone, and it often motivates a repair. It is usually a helpful signal that you can make things right.
Shame says I am a bad person, and it tends to make people hide or withdraw. Because it targets identity, it is harder to resolve.
Guilt has a clear next step: apologise, fix the error or make amends. When you notice shame, return to the specific behaviour and ask what it needs.

fig.title: Guilt or shame?
fig.note: Guilt points to an action you can change. Shame points to your identity.

ex.q: You forgot a friend's birthday and feel bad for letting them down. Which feeling is this most likely?
ex.why: Feeling bad about one specific lapse is guilt, which focuses on an action you can repair. Shame would be a belief that you are a bad person overall.

lessons.tip: Guilt says I did a bad thing; shame says I am a bad person.

quiz.q: Which response is typical of guilt?
quiz.why: Guilt usually motivates repair, such as an apology or a fix for the specific mistake.

quiz.q: Why is shame harder to resolve?
quiz.why: Because shame attacks who you are rather than what you did, there is no single action that clears it.

lessons.intro: You will learn a short daily check-in that builds self-awareness in just a few minutes. Regular practice makes naming feelings a natural habit rather than an effort.

cards.b: Ten seconds of noticing, repeated several times a day, trains your attention faster than occasional deep reflection. Small repeated actions are more reliable than long sessions.

cards.h: Use a cue you already have
cards.b: Attach the check-in to something you do every day, such as the kettle boiling or sitting down at your desk. The existing routine reminds you without extra effort.
At the end of the day, recall the strongest feeling and what caused it. Writing one sentence about it helps you remember the lesson.

fig.title: Daily check-in loop
fig.note: Repeat the loop at three points each day.

ex.q: You want a daily check-in that sticks. Which approach is most likely to work?
o: Wait until you feel like it
Do one long session each month
Attach it to an existing daily habit
ex.why: Linking the check-in to an existing habit gives a reliable cue, which makes the practice more likely to stick. Waiting for motivation or doing rare long sessions usually fades.

lessons.tip: Attach your check-in to something you already do every day.

quiz.q: When is a good time for an evening reflection?
o: Just before a big exam only
At the end of the day
quiz.why: The end of the day is a natural point to recall the strongest feeling and its cause.

quiz.q: What makes a check-in easier to keep?
o: Making it as long as possible
Doing it only once a year
Linking it to an existing cue
quiz.why: An existing daily cue reminds you without extra effort, which is why it helps habits stick.

lessons.t: Feelings rarely stay in one place
lessons.intro: You will learn that emotions move and change within a single situation. Seeing that change helps you avoid deciding how you feel about something based on one moment.

cards.b: A presentation can start with nerves, rise to pride and end in relief, all within an hour. Your feelings are a sequence, not a single fixed label.
Track how a feeling changed from start to finish of an event. Noticing the arc tells you what triggered each shift.
Avoid deciding how you feel about a job, person or plan from the first hour. Later information often changes the picture completely.

fig.title: A feeling that changes
fig.note: Feelings shift as new information arrives.

ex.q: You felt anxious before a talk, proud during it and relieved after. Which conclusion is most reasonable?
o: Emotions shifted as the event unfolded
The talk was a total failure
ex.why: Feelings changed in response to different stages of the event, so the sequence is the honest picture. The other options claim too much from a single feeling.

lessons.tip: Ask how you felt at the start, middle and end before judging an event.

quiz.q: What is the best reason to wait before judging an event?
o: Later information can change the picture
quiz.why: Later information often reshapes how an event looks, so early reactions may not be the final picture.

quiz.q: What does the sequence of feelings reveal?
quiz.why: Tracing the sequence shows which moments caused changes, which is useful for learning.

lessons.intro: You will learn to combine body signals, named feelings and underlying values into one short reading. Putting the three together gives you a fuller picture than any single clue.

cards.b: A body signal, a precise feeling name and an underlying value together explain most strong reactions. Each clue alone is partial, but the three together tell a clearer story.
Complete the sentence: My jaw is tight, so I feel anger, because fairness matters to me. Short readings are quick to write and easy to revisit.
Once you know what the feeling protects, pick a response that honours that value. For example, you might ask for a fair share of credit calmly.

fig.title: Linking signal, feeling and value
fig.note: Three clues together show what a strong feeling protects.

ex.q: Your chest feels heavy, you name the feeling as sadness, and you notice that connection matters most to you. What is the best one-line reading?
o: I am fine and nothing matters
My heavy chest shows sadness, because connection with others matters to me
ex.why: The reading links the body signal, the named feeling and the value it protects. The other options drop one clue or contradict the information.

lessons.tip: Three clues together make your self-reading far more accurate than one.

quiz.q: Which clue is NOT part of the three-clue reading?
quiz.why: The reading uses body signals, feeling names and values, not unrelated preferences like favourite films.

quiz.q: Why write a one-line reading?
o: It must be a long essay
It is quick to write and revisit
quiz.why: A short reading is easy to write, makes patterns visible, and is simple to return to.

lessons.intro: You will learn a simple pause that stands between a strong feeling and your reply. A short pause turns a reflex into a decision you can stand behind.

cards.h: The gap is where choice lives
cards.b: Between a trigger and a reaction there is a small gap of a few seconds. Learning to use that gap is the core skill of emotional regulation.
A pause of a few seconds, even just counting to six, gives the first surge of an urge time to settle. Use the time to look at the situation again.
A longer exhale tends to slow the heart and calm the body. Try breathing in for four counts and out for six.

fig.title: Pausing before a reply
fig.note: The pause is short, but it creates room for a deliberate choice.

ex.q: Someone says something sharp and you feel an urge to snap back. What is the best first move?
ex.why: Pausing and breathing out slowly creates space to decide how to respond. Snapping back is an immediate reaction that often escalates things.

lessons.tip: Count to six before you speak when a strong urge arrives.

quiz.q: Breathing in for four and out for six emphasises which part?
quiz.why: A longer exhale tends to slow the heart and calm the body.

quiz.q: What is the gap between trigger and reaction?
quiz.why: The small gap after a trigger is where you can choose a response rather than react automatically.

lessons.intro: You will learn how the intensity of a feeling affects how many responses you can see. Recognising high intensity tells you when to slow down before acting.

cards.b: When a feeling is very strong, you tend to see only one or two responses. Calm moments reveal a wider range of possible actions.
Give the feeling a number from one to ten before you decide what to do. If it is above seven, delay any important reply.
Reduce intensity with movement, cold water or a brief walk before tackling the issue. Once the number drops, your options return.

fig.title: Intensity narrows your options
fig.note: Ratings out of ten, from calm to furious.

ex.q: You rate your anger at nine out of ten and feel ready to send an angry email. What is the wisest step?
o: Send it now while it is strong
Delay and lower the intensity first
ex.why: High intensity narrows your options, so delaying until the feeling drops gives you a clearer choice. Sending it at nine out of ten usually leads to regret.

lessons.tip: If the number is high, the decision can wait until it drops.

quiz.q: At what rating might you delay a reply?
quiz.why: Ratings above seven suggest the feeling is strong enough to narrow your choices, so pausing helps.

quiz.q: What is a quick way to lower intensity?
quiz.why: A short walk or movement often lowers arousal quickly, letting you see your options again.

lessons.intro: You will learn the difference between pushing a feeling down and changing how you interpret it. Reinterpreting a situation tends to work better than suppressing it.

cards.b: Forcing a feeling out of sight takes effort, and the feeling often returns later. Studies on emotional suppression have found that it often does not reduce how strongly you feel.
Reappraisal means looking at a situation and asking what else it could mean. A missed call might mean a busy day rather than rejection.
Practise reframing on small annoyances, like a slow queue or a late bus. The skill grows through repetition and works best when a feeling is only moderate.

fig.title: Suppression or reappraisal
fig.note: Suppression hides the signal. Reappraisal changes its meaning.

ex.q: A colleague's email is curt. Which reappraisal is most reasonable?
o: They may be rushed, and the tone may not be personal
They hate my work for sure
ex.why: Reappraisal considers other plausible meanings, such as rushed writing. The other options assume a hostile motive without evidence.

lessons.tip: Ask what else this could mean before you settle on the worst story.

quiz.q: What does suppression do?
quiz.why: Suppression tries to hide the outward signs of a feeling rather than changing its meaning.

quiz.q: Which is an example of reappraisal?
o: Forcing a smile and saying nothing
Considering that a late reply may mean a busy day
quiz.why: Reappraisal reinterprets the situation, such as seeing a late reply as a busy day rather than a snub.

lessons.intro: You will learn a four-part cycle for handling a difficult moment calmly. Working through the cycle in order keeps you from jumping straight to action.

cards.b: Put a label on what you feel, even silently, to create distance from it. Research on affect labelling suggests that naming a feeling can reduce its intensity.
Ask what else the situation could mean and what the other person might need. A fresh interpretation usually produces a calmer and more useful reply.
After the moment passes, note which step helped and which did not. A quick review turns each difficult moment into practice for the next one.

fig.title: The regulation cycle
fig.note: Use the loop in tense moments and reflect on it afterwards.

ex.q: In a heated meeting you name your feeling, reframe the comment as a rushed remark, then choose a calm reply. What step is still missing from the cycle?
ex.why: The cycle ends with a review, which turns the experience into learning for next time. The other options do not complete the cycle.

lessons.tip: Finish every hard moment with one line about what helped.

quiz.q: Which step comes right after naming the feeling?
quiz.why: The cycle moves from naming the feeling to reframing the situation before choosing a response.

quiz.q: Why review after a tense moment?
o: To avoid any feelings ever again
quiz.why: A short review shows which steps worked, which makes the next difficult moment easier.

lessons.intro: You will learn to stay with an uncomfortable feeling for short, growing periods without acting on it. Tolerance grows through gradual practice rather than sudden force.

cards.b: An uncomfortable feeling is unpleasant but usually not harmful, even when it is intense. Reminding yourself of this lowers the urge to escape immediately.
Start by sitting with a mild feeling for one minute, then extend the time gradually. Each success makes the next step feel more manageable.

cards.h: Notice the feeling rise and fall
cards.b: Feelings usually peak and then ease within minutes if you do not feed them. Watching the wave pass teaches you that discomfort does not last forever.

fig.title: Growing practice time
fig.note: Gradually lengthen the time you sit with a feeling.

ex.q: You want to build tolerance for mild worry. Which plan is best?
o: Sit with mild worry for one minute, then extend
ex.why: Starting small and gradually extending time builds tolerance safely. Jumping to the hardest situation or avoiding entirely does not build it.

lessons.tip: Sit with a feeling for one minute longer than you usually would.

quiz.q: What usually happens to a strong feeling that is not fed?
o: It peaks and eases within minutes
quiz.why: Intense feelings usually rise, peak and ease within minutes when they are not fed by further action.

quiz.q: How should tolerance be built?
quiz.why: Gradual, growing practice builds tolerance more reliably than sudden exposure.

lessons.t: Matching a tool to an urge
lessons.intro: You will learn to match a regulation tool to the specific feeling you are dealing with. Different feelings respond to different tools, so a small menu helps you choose quickly.

cards.h: Match the tool to the feeling
cards.b: Anger often responds well to a pause and movement, while worry responds well to writing things down. Choosing a tool that fits the feeling makes it more effective.
Write down three to five tools that have worked for you before. Keep the list where you can see it when stress arrives.
Use a tool for about five minutes and rate your feeling again. If it did not help, switch to another tool rather than pushing harder.

fig.title: Matching a tool to an urge
fig.note: Pick the tool that fits the feeling you are having.

ex.q: You feel worried about tomorrow's exam. Which tool is the best match?
ex.why: Writing specific worries turns vague dread into concrete items you can plan for. The other options either escalate arousal or ignore the feeling.

lessons.tip: Carry two or three tools that you already know work for you.

quiz.q: How long should you try one tool before assessing it?
quiz.why: Trying a tool for about five minutes is enough to see whether your feeling has shifted.

quiz.q: If a tool does not help, what should you do?
o: Push harder with the same tool
quiz.why: Switching to a different tool is more useful than pushing harder with one that is not working.

lessons.intro: You will learn a short physical sequence that lowers arousal before you try to think clearly. Calming the body first makes it much easier to reason through the problem.

cards.b: When the body is aroused, logical thinking becomes harder even when you know better. Calming physical tension first makes reasoning easier.
Tense each muscle group for five seconds, then release it slowly. The contrast helps you notice the difference between tension and ease.
Sit tall, let your feet rest on the floor and lower your gaze slightly. Small posture changes often reduce the sense of threat.

fig.title: A body-first calming sequence
fig.note: Start with the body, then return to your thoughts.

ex.q: Your heart is racing before a difficult call. What should you do first to think more clearly?
o: Calm the body with slow breathing
ex.why: Calming arousal through slow breathing helps the thinking brain come back online. Rushing into argument while aroused tends to make reasoning harder.

lessons.tip: Relax your jaw and shoulders before you open your mouth.

quiz.q: What is the first step in the sequence?
quiz.why: The sequence begins with softening the face and then moves through the shoulders and breath.

quiz.q: Why calm the body before reasoning?
o: High arousal makes clear thinking harder
quiz.why: When the body is aroused, reasoning is harder, so settling physical tension comes first.

lessons.intro: You will learn how to check whether a regulation tool is actually lowering your intensity. Simple before and after ratings show you which methods help you personally.

cards.b: Rate your feeling before using a tool and again afterwards. The difference tells you more than any general advice about what should work.
A helpful tool often drops a rating by one or two points rather than eliminating the feeling. Small drops add up across many moments.
Note the tools that consistently reduce your rating and use them first. Drop the ones that leave you no calmer after several tries.

fig.title: Tension before and after a walk
fig.note: Example ratings out of ten, showing a drop after movement.

ex.q: Your tension is 8 before a walk and 5 after. How much did it drop?
ex.why: The drop is 8 minus 5, which equals 3 points. So the walk lowered your tension by three points.

lessons.tip: A drop of two or three points is a real win worth repeating.

quiz.q: What is 15 minus 9?
quiz.why: Fifteen minus nine equals six.

quiz.q: Which tool should you keep using?
o: The one that makes you more tense
The one that lowers your rating consistently
quiz.why: Tools that consistently lower your own rating are the ones worth keeping for your personal routine.

lessons.intro: You will learn how to respond to frustration in a way that is honest without being hostile. Assertive replies protect your needs while keeping the relationship intact.

cards.b: An assertive reply says what you need, calmly and specifically, without blaming the other person. It treats your needs and theirs as equally worth respecting.
Try a sentence like: I felt unheard when the decision changed, and I need to talk about it. This focuses on your experience rather than their character.
Wait until your rating drops below about five before you raise a serious point. A calm reply usually lands far better than an immediate one.

fig.title: Aggressive or assertive?
fig.note: Assertive replies name the need without attacking the person.

ex.q: A colleague keeps interrupting you. Which reply is most assertive?
o: When I am interrupted, I lose my thread, so please let me finish this point
I will just stay quiet forever
ex.why: The assertive reply names the effect on you and asks for a specific change without attacking the person. The other options are aggressive or passive.

lessons.tip: Say what you need in one clear sentence, then listen.

quiz.q: Which describes an assertive reply?
quiz.why: Assertiveness combines clarity with calm respect for both people involved.

quiz.q: What is an I statement?
o: A sentence about your own experience and need
quiz.why: I statements describe your experience and need rather than attacking the other person.

lessons.intro: You will learn how to recover when you react badly despite your best efforts. Recovery matters as much as prevention because everyone slips sometimes.

cards.b: Even skilled people sometimes snap or sulk, especially when tired or stressed. Expecting this lowers the shame that often makes recovery harder.
A simple apology that names what you did, without excuses, helps repair trust. For example, I raised my voice earlier, and I am sorry for that.
Ask what led to the slip and what you would try next time. Small adjustments, such as taking a walk earlier, reduce future slips.

fig.title: Recovering after a slip
fig.note: Recovery is a skill you practise, not a single event.

ex.q: You snapped at a friend and later realise you were tired and overloaded. What is the best recovery step?
o: Blame your friend for the snap
Apologise briefly and name what you did
ex.why: A brief, specific apology repairs trust without excuses or blame. Pretending nothing happened or avoiding them tends to let the tension grow.

lessons.tip: Repair a slip within a day, while the moment is still fresh.

quiz.q: What makes an apology more effective?
quiz.why: Naming the specific action shows you understand the impact and makes the repair credible.

quiz.q: What do you ask after a slip?
o: How do I forget it fast
What led to it and what I would change
quiz.why: Reviewing the trigger and a change for next time turns a slip into learning.

lessons.intro: You will learn how repeated small pauses can steadily bring a strong feeling down over an hour. Sustained calm comes from many small choices rather than one heroic effort.

cards.b: Repeated short pauses can bring a rating down step by step rather than in one dramatic leap. The total effect of several small choices is often large.
During a long meeting or journey, check your feeling every half hour and note the rating. Regular checks stop a slow build from going unnoticed.

cards.h: Plan breaks before you need them
cards.b: Schedule a two-minute reset between demanding tasks rather than waiting for overwhelm. Planned breaks protect your regulation when the day gets hard.

fig.title: Ratings falling with each pause
fig.note: Each pause can lower your rating by a point or two.

ex.q: Your anger goes from 9 to 7, then to 5. What is the total drop after these two steps?
ex.why: Each step drops the rating by two points, so 9 to 7 and then 7 to 5 gives a total drop. Nine minus five equals four points.

lessons.tip: Track the number as you go so small drops become visible.

quiz.q: What is 12 minus 5?
quiz.why: Twelve minus five equals seven.

quiz.q: What is a good interval for checking in during a long meeting?
quiz.why: Checking about every half hour catches a slow build before it grows.

lessons.intro: You will learn to plan your regulation practice across a week rather than leaving it to chance. A simple plan turns good intentions into a routine you can actually follow.

cards.b: Look at your calendar and mark the days that usually feel heavy. Place your strongest tools near those days so they are ready when you need them.

cards.h: Pair each focus with one tool
cards.b: For each pressure point, choose one tool from your toolkit and write it down. Having a single default reduces decision fatigue in the moment.
On Sunday, check which plan items you used and which felt useless. Swap the weak items and keep the ones that actually lowered your ratings.

fig.title: A weekly regulation plan
fig.note: Match a focus area to a tool you already trust.

ex.q: Your heaviest day is Friday because of a deadline. Which plan is most sensible?
o: Pick one strong tool and plan it for Friday
Add ten tools all at once
ex.why: Planning one strong tool for your known pressure point makes it ready when needed. Ten tools at once would be hard to remember and use.

lessons.tip: Put your best tool on the day you expect to struggle most.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a weekly plan?
o: To turn intentions into a routine
quiz.why: A plan turns good intentions into a repeatable routine you can follow.

quiz.q: When should you review your plan?
o: Each week, for example on Sunday
quiz.why: A weekly review lets you keep tools that work and swap ones that do not.

lessons.intro: You will learn to listen in a way that helps another person feel understood. Understanding someone's view starts with listening fully before you prepare a reply.

cards.b: Many people plan their reply while the other person is still speaking. Give your full attention first, and notice what they say and how they say it.
Repeat the main idea in your own words, such as: So you felt overlooked when the plan changed. This shows you are trying to understand rather than to win.
Questions starting with how or what invite fuller answers than yes or no questions do. For example, what worried you most about the change?

fig.title: Listening to understand
fig.note: Each step shows the other person that you are following them.

ex.q: A friend says they are exhausted from caring for a parent. Which response best shows listening?
o: That is nothing, I had it worse
Let me tell you my own story
It sounds really draining. What has been the hardest part?
ex.why: Naming the feeling and asking an open question invites your friend to share more. The other options redirect attention to you or offer unsolicited advice.

lessons.tip: Reflect before you respond, so the other person knows you heard them.

quiz.q: Which is an open question?
quiz.why: How did the meeting go invites a full answer, while the others can be answered with yes or no.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of reflecting back?
o: To show you understood the core message
quiz.why: Reflecting shows the other person you are trying to understand their view.

lessons.intro: You will learn why two people can look at the same situation and rank what matters differently. Seeing the reasons behind a priority makes disagreements easier to understand.

cards.b: Someone who has been burned by a late delivery may value speed above all else. Past experience often explains a priority more than stubbornness does.
Find out what outcome the person most wants to avoid or preserve. A clear answer usually reveals a shared goal beneath different methods.
Most disagreements sit on top of a goal both people actually share. Naming that goal first lowers defensiveness and opens practical options.

fig.title: Priorities in one project meeting
fig.note: Example scores out of ten for one person's priorities.

ex.q: In the bars, which priority scores highest, and what does it suggest?
o: Cost, so everyone should be cheap
Speed, so this person may value quick delivery
ex.why: Speed has the highest score at nine out of ten, suggesting it matters most to this person. The other options draw conclusions the chart does not support.

lessons.tip: Before you disagree, ask what the other person is protecting.

quiz.q: What is 9 minus 7?
quiz.why: Nine minus seven equals two, the gap between speed and quality in the example scores.

quiz.q: What usually sits beneath a disagreement?
quiz.why: Most disagreements are over methods, while both people often share a goal beneath them.

lessons.intro: You will learn to notice when you are assuming the worst about someone's intent. Asking for context often reveals a more ordinary explanation than the one you feared.

cards.b: When information is missing, the mind quickly fills gaps with the most dramatic story. Those stories feel true but are often incomplete.
Try a question like: Can you help me understand what happened with the report? This invites their side before you judge it.
Treat your interpretation as one possibility among several. Stay open to new information even after you have formed a first view.

fig.title: Assuming intent or seeking context
fig.note: Assumptions close the door. Questions open it.

ex.q: A teammate missed a deadline and did not message you. Which response best seeks context?
o: They clearly do not care about us
Ask them what got in the way and whether they need help
ex.why: Asking what got in the way opens the picture before you assign blame. The other options jump to a conclusion without information.

lessons.tip: Ask one curious question before you decide what someone meant.

quiz.q: What fills gaps when information is missing?
quiz.why: Without information the mind quickly writes a story, often a dramatic one.

quiz.q: Which is a context question?
quiz.why: Asking for their side invites explanation, while the others accuse or assume.

lessons.intro: You will learn a short routine for imagining how a situation looks from another person's side. Practising this loop helps you respond to people as they are rather than as you expect them to be.

cards.b: Ask what they were likely expecting, worrying about or hoping for before this happened. Their starting point often explains much of their reaction.
Your imagined view is a hypothesis, so test it gently in conversation. Saying I wonder if you were worried about the deadline invites correction.
Use what you learned to shape a reply that meets their concern while still stating your own needs. Kindness and honesty can work together.

fig.title: Perspective check loop
fig.note: Run the loop before you reply to a difficult message.

ex.q: A client sounds short in an email. Which perspective step is most useful first?
o: Imagine what they may be worried about
Reply with the same short tone
ex.why: Imagining their starting point, such as pressure or a missed deadline, helps you read the message more fairly. Matching the tone or assuming rudeness skips that step.

lessons.tip: Imagine their starting point before judging their ending point.

quiz.q: What is a hypothesis about another person's view?
quiz.why: Your imagined view is a guess, which you can check by asking gently.

quiz.q: What does kindness and honesty together allow?
o: Meeting their concern while stating your needs
quiz.why: You can respond to their concern while still being honest about what you need.

lessons.intro: You will learn to widen the range of viewpoints you consider in a situation. Each new perspective adds detail, which makes your understanding more accurate and fair.

cards.b: Most situations involve several people with different stakes, not just you and one other person. Listing everyone involved helps you spot viewpoints you might miss.

cards.h: Ask what each person gains or risks
cards.b: Consider what each person stands to gain, lose or fear from the outcome. Their stakes shape the views they hold, even when they never say so.

cards.h: Seek one new view each week
cards.b: Read a perspective you do not share, or talk with someone with a different background. Regular exposure widens the way you naturally see things.

fig.title: Widening the circle of views
fig.note: Consider each viewpoint, then the whole group.

ex.q: A project decision affects a designer, a client and a support team. What is the most complete first step?
o: Count how many meetings are scheduled
List all three groups and their stakes
ex.why: Listing everyone and their stakes gives a fuller view than focusing on one person. The other options narrow the view or skip the question entirely.

lessons.tip: Name at least three people affected before you decide anything.

quiz.q: How many people did the worked example involve?
quiz.why: The example names three groups: a designer, a client and a support team.

quiz.q: What does a widened view do?
quiz.why: Considering more perspectives makes your understanding richer and fairer, though it does not remove all disagreement.

lessons.intro: You will learn that body language and tone are clues, not proof, of what someone feels. Checking several possible meanings keeps you from reading too much into one signal.

cards.b: A frown can mean anger, concentration or simply bright sunlight. Treat nonverbal signals as hints that need checking before you act on them.
Before settling on one reading, list two or three other plausible explanations. This habit protects you from the most dramatic option.
Say what you noticed and ask about it, such as: You seem quiet, is something on your mind? This lets the person clarify rather than guess.

fig.title: Cues often have several meanings
fig.note: Any single cue could point to more than one cause.

ex.q: A colleague who is usually chatty goes quiet in a meeting. Which reading is best?
o: They are definitely angry at you
They might be thinking, tired or worried, so check gently
ex.why: Quiet has several plausible causes, so checking gently is better than assuming. The other options choose one dramatic reading without evidence.

lessons.tip: Check a cue with words before you act on it.

quiz.q: Which is a good first step with an unclear cue?
quiz.why: Gently asking lets the other person clarify rather than forcing you to guess.

quiz.q: Why hold several meanings open?
o: It proves you are always right
It protects you from the most dramatic reading
quiz.why: Listing alternatives stops one dramatic guess from taking over your understanding.

lessons.intro: You will learn a sequence for disagreeing with someone while still showing that you understand them. Respectful disagreement keeps the conversation useful rather than defensive.

cards.b: Summarise what the other person believes in a fair form before you offer your own. People accept disagreement far more readily when they feel accurately heard.
Look for the goal, value or fact you both share, even if your methods differ. Naming common ground makes the disagreement feel like teamwork.
Identify the specific point where you actually diverge, rather than the whole issue. Narrow disagreements are easier to resolve than broad ones.

fig.title: Disagreeing with respect
fig.note: Work through the steps in order before you argue your case.

ex.q: Your colleague wants a weekly meeting and you think it wastes time. Which opening is most respectful?
o: You want a clear update, and I think a shorter format could also work
ex.why: Naming the shared goal of a clear update, then offering a different format, respects their view while making your point. The other options dismiss their view.

lessons.tip: Restate the other view fairly before you add your own.

quiz.q: What comes first in respectful disagreement?
quiz.why: Restating their view shows you have understood it before you offer your own.

quiz.q: What makes a disagreement easier to resolve?
quiz.why: A narrow difference gives both people a clear point to work on together.

lessons.intro: You will learn to notice how much of a conversation you are taking up, and how to leave space for the other person. Balanced airtime is a simple sign that you are truly listening.

cards.b: Think about how much of a conversation you spend speaking compared with listening. Many people overestimate their listening, especially when they feel strongly.
After the other person finishes, wait a moment before replying to allow more to come out. Silence often invites a deeper point than a quick response.
Hold back interruptions, even when you think you know the answer. Interrupting signals that your view matters more than theirs.

fig.title: Airtime in a ten-minute chat
fig.note: A balanced chat often gives the other person most of the airtime.

ex.q: In a ten-minute chat you spoke for seven minutes. How many minutes did the other person speak, if the rest was theirs?
ex.why: Ten minutes minus seven minutes of your speaking leaves three minutes for them. A balanced chat would give them more time than that in many cases.

lessons.tip: Count your talking minutes once and you will notice the imbalance.

quiz.q: What is 10 minus 4?
quiz.why: Ten minus four equals six.

quiz.q: What signals that your view matters more?
quiz.why: Interrupting shows you are prioritising your own view over theirs.

lessons.intro: You will learn how empathy, which means understanding from inside someone's experience, differs from sympathy, which means caring from a distance. Knowing the difference helps you respond in the way people actually need.

cards.b: Empathy means imagining and sharing the emotional experience of another person. It asks you to understand what the situation feels like from inside.
Sympathy is caring about someone's difficulty while staying outside their experience. It is valuable, but it can sound like pity if offered in the wrong moment.

cards.h: Match the response to the need
cards.b: Some people need you to understand, while others need practical help. Ask what would be most useful before offering a fix.

fig.title: Empathy and sympathy differ

pts: Tries to feel what they feel

fig.note: Both are kind, but empathy works from inside their experience.

ex.q: A friend says they feel overwhelmed by work. Which reply shows empathy most clearly?
o: Sounds like the workload has been crushing you. Do you want to vent or problem-solve?
ex.why: The empathic reply names the feeling from inside their experience and checks what they need. The other options minimise or dismiss the feeling.

lessons.tip: Ask whether someone wants to be understood or helped before you offer a fix.

quiz.q: What is empathy?
o: Understanding a feeling from inside someone's experience
quiz.why: Empathy means sharing an understanding of the feeling from within the other person's experience.

quiz.q: Why check what someone needs?
o: So you can end the chat
So your help is useful to them
So you never have to listen
quiz.why: Matching your response to the real need makes your help more useful.

lessons.intro: You will learn to keep your empathy active even when a conversation becomes tense. Staying curious under pressure helps both people move toward a workable solution.

cards.b: When you feel attacked, your instinct is to defend or counter rather than to understand. Knowing this makes it easier to catch the moment and choose differently.
Saying that someone's concern makes sense does not mean you agree with every part. Validation lowers defensiveness, so problem-solving becomes possible.
End with a question such as: What would a good outcome look like for you? This keeps the conversation moving toward shared solutions.

fig.title: Empathy under pressure
fig.note: Repeat the loop as the conversation moves.

ex.q: A client is furious about a delay. Which first step keeps empathy active?
o: Name their frustration and let them describe the impact
Explain why it is not your fault
ex.why: Naming the frustration and letting them describe the impact shows you understand before you explain. The other options defend, abandon or commit to a fix before understanding the problem.

lessons.tip: Validate the feeling first, even if you dispute the facts.

quiz.q: Does validating a concern mean you agree with everything?
o: No, it means it makes sense from their side
quiz.why: Validation acknowledges that the concern makes sense without endorsing every claim.

quiz.q: What kind of question keeps the talk moving?
o: What would a good outcome look like for you?
quiz.why: An outcome question invites shared solutions rather than blame or escalation.

lessons.intro: You will learn how empathy becomes a habit when you practise small skills consistently. Over time, listening, asking and checking become automatic in everyday conversations.

cards.b: People are not simply born with empathy or without it; the skill grows with practice. Each careful conversation adds a little to your ability.
Choose one habit, such as asking one open question per conversation, and do it for two weeks. A single focus is easier to sustain than many changes at once.
Look for small signs of growth, such as catching yourself before interrupting. Recognising progress keeps motivation steady over the long term.

fig.title: The empathy habit loop
fig.note: Each small habit feeds the next one.

ex.q: You want to become more empathic in daily chats. Which plan is most realistic?
o: Pick one habit, like asking an open question, for two weeks
ex.why: A single habit practised for two weeks is realistic and builds steadily. Trying to master everything at once usually leads to giving up.

lessons.tip: Pick one empathy habit and practise it in every conversation this week.

quiz.q: Is empathy a fixed trait or a learned skill?
o: A learned skill that grows with practice
A fixed trait you cannot change
A rare gift only for some
quiz.why: Empathy is a skill people can strengthen through regular practice.

quiz.q: How long does the lesson suggest focusing on one habit?
quiz.why: Two weeks on a single habit is a realistic window to build consistency.

lessons.intro: You will learn how the three skills of self-awareness, regulation and empathy work together in one routine. Seeing them as a connected set makes them easier to use under pressure.

cards.b: You cannot calm a feeling you have not noticed, so self-awareness comes first. Labelling a feeling creates the space in which regulation can happen.
When you are calm, you can listen to someone else without becoming defensive. Pausing gives you room to consider their view.
Understanding another view often reveals new information about your own feelings. The three skills keep feeding each other across daily life.

fig.title: Your three-skill emotional toolkit
fig.note: Each module builds a skill that the next one relies on.

ex.q: Which order best describes how the three skills build on one another?
ex.why: Awareness comes first so you can notice, regulation lets you respond calmly, and empathy then lets you understand others. The other orders skip a dependency.

lessons.tip: Notice, steady, then understand: that is the order to practise.

quiz.q: What comes first in the three skills?
quiz.why: You need to notice your own feeling before you can regulate or fully understand others.

quiz.q: What does regulation make possible for empathy?
quiz.why: When you are calm, you can hear another view without immediately defending yourself.
